blogs.content: Jev: For the builders AND dreamers - TypeSafe AI Blog TypeSafe AI Enterprise Thoughts Company Docs API console Contact us API console Docs Menu ∵ Back Company News Company News Jev: For the builders AND dreamers Oct 14, 2026 Oct 14, 2026 Oct 14, 2026 TL;DR: We're releasing an improved Jev 1.14.0 along with experimental features for our dreamers: images, a new type, and longer context. Enter the danger zone at your own risk. 🔥 Our philosophy A huge debate we’ve been having is on the balance between reliability and creativity. To really care about the prod builders, we should be shipping models that meet our quality bar for intelligence and have been battle-tested to the limits of what we can do internally. On the other hand, there’s no way that our team has a full understanding of what is needed to spark delight in the world and build sick sci-fi. We don’t want to impose our values of extreme reliability on those dreamers. Our solution: share those dreamer-ready features under “danger zone” flags in our API headers. These are features that will be here to stay for future models, are (as far as we can tell) better than what exists out there, and will continue to get better by leaps and bounds. But as a warning, we think there is still way too much jaggedness for us to vouch for these for production use cases! See these new capabilities as a continuation of what we’ve built over 2 years of stealth. They’re less ready for automation, but very fun to play with. They’re also an early glimpse into what we’re focused on making reliable enough to meet TypeSafe standards. Composable Images Not only are we enabling multimodality for future Jev models, we’re enabling it for the current Jev that you all know and love. Surprise: the Jev you all know and love ( jev-1.13.0 ) was multimodal all along! Image support is fully composable via a find-and-replace in assets . You can put them anywhere that our JSON interface supports: in the state , instructions , or even criteria ! Play around with it, push the boundaries of technology, and let us know where Jev can improve. As a warning, all models (Jev included) perform worse on multimodality over pure text. Breaking down questions into the simplest possible decompositions helps a lot. TypeSafe-Danger-Zone-Images: true Check out docs: docs.typesafe.ai/go/images Types Beyond Decisions We’re introducing another new type as well: box . It returns a single bounding box - no type errors allowed. It’s our first type that’s not purely meant for smart-if statements, and is a preview for our explorations beyond simple decisions into what else System One Models can support. We made huge leaps and bounds on this one recently, so we’re enabling this only for jev-1.14.0 (spoilers). Check out docs: docs.typesafe.ai/go/box Size does matter, apparently 💅 We’ve heard you loud and clear on context lengths. Jev actually supports a much longer context length than we’ve enabled in production. We chose to limit it intentionally because Jev, like all models, is less reliable on longer contexts, and this constraint encourages more effective usage patterns in prod. We aren’t your parents though, so while we strongly recommend limiting context length, you no longer have to: TypeSafe-Danger-Zone-Long-Context: true Check out docs: docs.typesafe.ai/models#context-length Opt-in to help us We love the community’s desire to help make models better! We’ve added an opt-in to allow you to help find model jaggedness with your queries. We will still not train on your queries, but this does make it easier for us to find issues and help debug your use cases. jev-1.14.0 We’re also releasing a new version of Jev under jev-preview ! Not meant to be flashy but instead be small, subtle improvements to everything . Most things should be a tiny bit better, but we expect the largest gain in multi-lingual support. blogs.content: How Jack & Jill Cut Candidate Screening Costs By 88% With Jev - TypeSafe AI Blog TypeSafe AI Enterprise Thoughts Company Docs API console Contact us API console Docs Menu ∵ Back Case Study Case Study ')"> How Jack & Jill Cut Candidate Screening Costs By 88% With Jev Oct 7, 2026 Oct 7, 2026 Oct 7, 2026 We saved ~half a million dollars last week with Jev. And our products got much better at the same time. Matthew Wilson, Co-founder/CEO @ Jack & Jill View post on LinkedIn Background Jack & Jill is a talent marketplace brokered by AI agents. Jack is a career agent for top professionals and Jill is an agent for hiring teams. When Jack and Jill agree there is a mutual match, they introduce the candidate and the company directly, skipping the application altogether. To date, they’ve worked with over 5,000 companies and more than 400,000 professionals working in startups - and raised a total of $60M in the process. Within 10 days of their first test, Jack & Jill had fully rolled out Jev in production - replacing Gemini 3.1 Flash Lite for 100% of calls for a key stage in their candidate matching pipeline. Compared to Gemini, Jev maintained the same level of accuracy, with 88% lower cost and roughly 50% faster task completion time. Cost savings are projected to be $500K per year - and more importantly, new use cases have been unlocked across the product, such as showing candidates matched jobs immediately after signup. Impact Result Details ↓ $500K/year Absolute projected savings ↓ 88% cost BEFORE | $0.755 with Google Gemini AFTER | $0.092 with TypeSafe Jev Cost per 1,000 candidates scored 2x speed BEFORE | 20.3 sec AFTER | 10.3 sec Median time to screen each candidate No loss in quality BEFORE | 93.9% Baseline AFTER | 94.6% Candidates requested by hiring managers The challenge: expensive to screen a large volume of candidates with Gemini Before Jev Candidate pool. Every day, 6,000 candidates for every open role are pulled from the database Initial scoring. A low-cost model (Gemini 3.1 Flash Lite) scores each candidate and creates a shortlist of the top 2,000 candidates Close review. A higher-power model assesses the top 2,000 candidates, ending with a list of a few hundred candidates for the hiring manager Even with a “low-cost” model like Gemini Flash Lite, costs were adding up fast, due to the "Initial scoring" step that assessed 6,000 candidates for every open role. Results with Jev: Similar quality to Gemini at 88% lower cost With Jev Before switching, Jack & Jill tested both Gemini and Jev models on 150 live roles, and the same candidates for each role. For each role, they included: every past “winner”: a candidate a hiring manager later asked to meet a sample of remaining candidates (weighted to accurately represent the original 6,000 candidates retrieved for each role) The test counted how many winners each model kept on the shortlist. For example, a score of 95% means that for every 100 candidates that the hiring manager asked to be introduced to, the model correctly kept 95 of them in its shortlist. Ultimately, Jack & Jill found that Jev was able to maintain similar quality to Gemini, with 88% lower cost and half the median time to complete scoring. Overall, the team expects to save more than $500K based on projected volumes over the next 12 months. Quality: Slightly higher than Gemini (Recall and AUC) Jev kept slightly more winning candidates than Gemini (+0.7 percentage points), although the difference was not statistically significant (90% confidence interval of −0.4 to +1.8) Jev also performed slightly better on AUC, a measure of how often a model ranks a winner above a randomly chosen candidate with no recorded hiring manager selection. 1.0 is perfect and 0.5 is a coin toss. Jev’s score of 0.933 means it ranked the winner higher in approximately 93.3% of those pairings, compared with 92.4% for Gemini — aligning better with the recorded hiring manager selections. blogs.description: TypeSafe AI is an AI lab building machine-native intelligence infrastructure for automation, designed to make decisions within software. Try our first System One Model, Jev, in early access.
blogs.content: Introducing System One Models & Jev - TypeSafe AI Blog TypeSafe AI Enterprise Thoughts Company Docs API console Contact us API console Docs Menu ∵ Back Company News Company News Introducing System One Models & Jev Sep 15, 2026 Sep 15, 2026 Sep 15, 2026 Diogo Almeida, founder, TypeSafe Models have been superhuman at chat for years, so where is all the automation? This has been my driving question for the last four years. At OpenAI, I helped build the methods that made language models useful at following instructions and talking with people. That work ended up as the research behind ChatGPT. At the time, I thought maybe chat models would lead to AGI, but despite the hype it became obvious to me that there was something really big missing. After two years in stealth, countless technical challenges, and research breakthroughs… I am beyond excited to announce that today, TypeSafe AI is releasing our first System One Model : a new class of frontier models built to make fast, structured decisions that software can use directly. We built a new stack entirely focused on automation: with a new model architecture, parallel sampler for maximum efficiency, and training method we call Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Decisions (RLCD). Our first public model is Jev , available today in early access. Jev achieves similar levels of intelligence on System One tasks compared to existing LLMs, while being two orders of magnitude faster and more efficient. While Jev gives up string generation, it’s optimized for structured outputs and can’t hallucinate. Think of Jev as a frontier-intelligence function call: unstructured state in, typed probabilistic decisions out. Extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence so see below for the receipts. 💅 Frontiers, Old and New Existing LLMs System One + Jev Optimized with Reinforcement Learning with Human Feedback (RLHF) / Reinforcement Learning with Verifiable Rewards (RLVR) Reinforcement Learning for Calibrated Decisions (RLCD) Optimizes for Human preference: writeups and chat responses that human raters prefer. Verifiable rewards: outputs that can be programmatically verified. Calibrated decisions: answers with epistemically honest probabilities on System One tasks. Inputs Unstructured data (e.g. text) with an emphasis on sequential messages . Unstructured data (e.g. text) with an emphasis on structured program state . Outputs Strings / generated text. Strings are flexible and can be anything: chat responses, code, hallucinations, refusals, or even type-safe structured values. To be used by software, responses need to be parsed + validated. There is also always some risk that the AI goes off the rails. Type-safe structured values. Possible outputs and structure are defined in advance . The model never makes type errors. All answers are accompanied with calibrated probabilities and confidence scores. Sampling Sequential. Generates one token at a time, each conditioned on the last. Parallel. Generates all outputs in a single query. Incredibly efficient and hardware-aware. Cost Input tokens: from $0.20 to $10 / MTok. Output tokens: ~5x more expensive than input tokens. Input tokens: $0.042 / MTok ($42 per billion tokens). Output tokens: FREE (too cheap to meter). Speed End-to-end response time is 3 to 329 seconds for frontier models. Fast enough for interfacing with humans, but a big bottleneck when integrated in code. End-to-end response time is 70ms-500ms for TypeSafe. This can range from 40x-200x faster for the same levels of frontier intelligence for System One shaped queries. Confidence Even if prompted for a confidence estimate, models tend to be overconfident and inconsistent. If a model can do a task 95% of the time but doesn’t say when it’s in the 5%, it can’t automate that task. Always communicates confidence and uncertainty with every output. Calibrated: higher confidence means higher accuracy. More consistent: returns similar answers for similar inputs. Use cases Human-in-the-loop tasks

blogs.description: TypeSafe AI is an AI lab building machine-native intelligence infrastructure for automation, designed to make decisions within software. Try our first System One Model, Jev, in early access.
blogs.content: Lies, Damned Lies, and Benchmarks - TypeSafe AI Blog TypeSafe AI Enterprise Thoughts Company Docs API console Contact us API console Docs Menu ∵ Back Thoughts Thoughts Lies, Damned Lies, and Benchmarks Sep 11, 2026 Sep 11, 2026 Sep 11, 2026 Benchmarks got us to incredibly smart AI. What gets measured gets managed, and for years making lots of benchmark numbers go up generally made models smarter. I’m not arguing against benchmarks and their helpful contributions to progress. I’m against benchmaxxing. A benchmark inevitably gets “benchmaxxed” when people building the model can optimize for a public eval score[1]. You don’t have to train directly on a benchmark to benchmaxx it; you just have to train on similar data or try a hundred experimental settings, then compare how your model performs. The benchmark selects the model even if nobody intended to game it. Things were not great when benchmarks were an academic pursuit, but now that they are tied to enormous attention and funding , negative incentives to game them abound. Illustration of the Streetlight Effect - source The field wants to measure general intelligence, but can only optimize what it can see. Public evals are the streetlight. Post-training therefore pushes capability fastest in the illuminated areas, while reliability outside them can stay flat or even get worse. My claim is that many of the spikes in “jagged intelligence” are the benchmarks. Annotated version from source Everyone is cheating Models chase benchmarks. Meta’s Llama 4 allegedly ranked near the top of LMArena , but it turned out that not only was it not the public model, Meta was also caught testing 27 private variants before picking the best one, which had the unusually verbose and emoji-heavy style that Arena users rewarded. The ordinary version later landed far lower . Even Claude (normally the goody two-shoes), on a benchmark to simulate a vending machine and end with the most money, formed price cartels, lied to suppliers and promised customer refunds it never sent. Benchmarks chase users. When GPT-6 Astra launched, Artificial Analysis’s Intelligence Index had it tied with GPT-5.6 Sol , which clashed with the widespread belief that Astra was a major leap. The next day, a revised index put Astra four points ahead . Three days later, another revision tied it with Claude Fable 5.1 for first . I do not think Artificial Analysis rigged the index. The changes are defensible. But the sequence shows the feedback loop: people’s intuitions about which model is better help determine whether an eval looks valid. The point of external evals should’ve been to inform the population, not the other way around. People cherry-pick for their favorite narrative. When the Chinese open-weight model GLM-5.2 beat Fable 5 on one web-design leaderboard, it became evidence that Chinese models had caught the frontier. Design Arena’s own analysis was narrower: GLM used more repeatable templates, generated 25% more code, took twice as long, and still lost to Fable on several design categories. Benchmarks have been broken for a while. Unspecialized humans scored 34.5% on MMLU in the original paper , worse than many small old models. The OpenAI coup was partially a result of safety researchers seeing models surpass PhD level at Google-Proof Question Answering (GPQA - an extremely hard dataset) in 2023. Yet humans still do most of the world’s useful work. Source Everyone in the field knows they’re broken, but they still get quoted because everyone is competing for attention. What benchmarks should be The crux of the problem is (1) intelligence is hard to measure, (2) a (good actor) lab wants to say “we made the model smarter,” and (3) for it to be believed (to whatever extent is accurate). Benchmarks are a shortcut to get around the hard problem of trust. They seem like a magnifier of trust, but instead are a loan: bad actors can then exploit the trust projected on the benchmark. The way out is to be trustworthy in the first plac

blogs.description: TypeSafe AI is an AI lab building machine-native intelligence infrastructure for automation, designed to make decisions within software. Try our first System One Model, Jev, in early access.
blogs.content: The Bitterest Lesson - TypeSafe AI Blog TypeSafe AI Enterprise Thoughts Company Docs API console Contact us API console Docs Menu ∵ Back Thoughts Thoughts The Bitterest Lesson Sep 10, 2026 Sep 10, 2026 Sep 10, 2026 TL;DR: Compute drives progress in AI, but what good is progress if you are not doing the right task! Rich Sutton’s bitter lesson states that compute beats algorithms. Researchers want to encode their clever ideas about intelligence into machines. Yet over and over, the approaches that win are the general ones which leverage more computation. Search beat hand-built chess knowledge. Neural networks beat hand-built vision features. The lesson is bitter because researchers love algorithms, yet cleverness matters less than scale. My experience is that Sutton’s bitter lesson is the tip of an iceberg of bitterer lessons: beyond compute and algorithms , there’s data and even picking the right task to do ML on. The bitterest lesson in ML is that doing the right task > data > compute > algorithms. Sutton’s bitter lesson is easiest to see in games because there are two major differences to the real world: the right task is obvious (follow the rules to win or maximize score), and data can be endlessly generated through self-play (through compute). It makes sense that the next most important thing is compute . At the end of the day, machine learning makes reward go up or loss go down. Someone still has to decide the objective to optimize though. Getting this right requires understanding the external system in which the model will operate. Without the right task, everything can work perfectly, with the most beautiful loss and scaling curves, but the model may still be useless! Unfortunately, ML research tends to attack these problems in the opposite order. Researchers love inventing algorithms. More recently, we have learned to love scaling curves. Meanwhile, data is messy. Choosing the right task often requires leaving the ML problem entirely to study users, products, organizations, or whatever part of the world is supposed to benefit. This is not an argument against scale. Once the task and data are right, scale is incredible. It is an argument against treating scale as the be-all and end-all. Bitter LLMs When life gives you LLMs... We learned this lesson at OpenAI when making InstructGPT/RLHF: GPT-3 was an incredible model trained to predict the next token on internet text, but people wanted something that followed instructions more than they wanted a super-powered autocomplete. GPT-2-sized models (>100x smaller than GPT-3) trained on the right task, 1 even with the dumbest algorithm 2 and barely any compute, destroyed GPT-3. Annotated from figure 31 from the InstructGPT paper Scaling pre-training would need to reach roughly GPT-7 level to beat even that baseline, and GPT-9 to beat InstructGPT built on GPT-3. 3 You get what you optimize for and the bitterest lesson in ML is that the most important part of it isn’t ML at all. ∵ ⩆ ⩆ ∵ TypeSafe AI © 2026 Contact Terms of Use Privacy Policy Acceptable Use Policy Accessibility LinkedIn X TypeSafe AI © 2026 Contact Terms of Use Privacy Policy Acceptable Use Policy Accessibility

blogs.content: The ten-year head start: How Stewart McKelvey got ready for AI before it arrived | Legora Product Solutions Security Customers Company Log in Book a demo Menu Log in Shapers The ten-year head start: How Stewart McKelvey got ready for AI before it arrived The ten-year head start: How Stewart McKelvey got ready for AI before it arrived Category Shapers published Oct 13, 2026 author Team Legora Lydia Bugden and Paul Saunders have spent more than a decade pursuing a shared vision for Stewart McKelvey, just from different seats. As CEO and Managing Partner, Lydia oversees the firm's six offices in Atlantic Canada, more than 250 lawyers, and over 350 staff on any given day. As Chief Strategy and Innovation Officer and Partner, Paul co-chairs the firm's AI and Technology Steering Committee, drives strategy and innovation across the firm, and is now Managing Director of Stewart McKelvey’s newest venture: the Fortified Firm. Eleven years ago, the two of them made the case to the firm's partnership board for something no one at Stewart McKelvey had done before: a dedicated practice innovation function. Its job was to systematically improve how the firm practiced law, covering everything from process and pricing to technology and profitability. They made that call years before generative AI existed, which is largely why the firm was ready to move fast once AI arrived to the business of law in a substantive way. Two different starting points, one shared instinct Lydia's path to leadership ran through in-house roles first. Those years gave her an early look at how good businesses are run, rather than just the legal work layered on top of them. Sitting on the client side meant understanding different law firms' value for herself, and taking on project work that stretched beyond legal advice into the operational side of the business. "They always let me do a little bit more than just the law," she says. "And I enjoyed that quite a bit." She became CEO and Managing Partner in August 2015, and has since been balancing the collegiality of a partnership alongside the discipline of running Atlantic Canada’s largest law firm. Early on, she pushed back when a senior partner insisted the firm was a partnership, not a business, telling him they were "professionals in a big business." This ability to see what's working ‘under the hood’ is what took her from evaluating outside counsel to running a substantial business. Paul came to law with a background in finance and technology. "I just started to look at opportunities to systematize, improve processes, solve problems," he says, recalling his first summer at work. Lydia noticed early. "Paul was the young lawyer you'd have someone pitch a virtual data room to for 50,000 US dollars," she says, "and he'd come in on a Monday and say, if you don't mind, I spent 18 dollars on a license, and here's a secure data room we can use. He'd solve the problem, but he'd also build something everyone else at the firm could use." By his fifth or sixth year practicing, Paul took a secondment to work on technology projects, and a trip to a legal conference in Chicago sharpened his sense of urgency. "I just couldn't believe what some of the conversations about profitability and leverage and pricing were, things we just weren't exploring at that point," he says. He came back and, in the fall of 2015, not long after Lydia became CEO, the two of them flew to St. John's to pitch creating a practice innovation role to the partnership board. Paul left his practice to become the firm's first Practice Innovation Partner, building out document automation, process mapping, and checklists. "It wasn't a hard sell," Lydia says. "Paul said he wanted to devote 100 percent of his time to the firm, and it just mushroomed from there." blogs.content: Meet the Legora engineer catching any problems that fall through the cracks | Legora Product Solutions Security Customers Company Log in Book a demo Menu Log in Legora voices Meet the Legora engineer catching any problems that fall through the cracks Meet the Legora engineer catching any problems that fall through the cracks Category Legora voices published Oct 7, 2026 author Team Legora Before becoming one of Legora's earliest engineering hires, Oskar Elvkull took a winding career path through auditing, energy tech, and backend development. Today, he's known at Legora for tackling the problems with no obvious owner, the unglamorous work that falls between the cracks but can make or break a company as it scales. Finding his way to Legora Oskar’s career started at EY, where he trained as an auditor before realizing that his real interest was in data. That led him to a Swedish energy startup, where he worked on building data infrastructure, and eventually into backend development. But Oskar's move to Legora was different. It wasn’t simply the role that convinced him to make the jump. It was the people and the way they thought. “It didn’t feel like a traditional interview. I was actually working on a coding problem, and it led to a really interesting discussion and sharing of ideas within the team. I knew after that meeting I had to be involved in building this company, and work alongside people who think the same way as me.” Being surrounded by people who are willing to question how things are done and figure things out together has continued to be a big focus when hiring new members of Oskar’s team as they scale. Scaling without losing the culture Oskar’s role has changed significantly over time as the company has grown. The engineering team has grown with it, but the culture that brought people together early on has remained remarkably consistent, with an emphasis on high standards, a willingness to take ownership and a shared appetite for constantly building. "When I joined, there were very skilled people, but the team was small. Now it's bigger, because the product's grown fast but the same energy is there. There's always someone to bounce ideas off, and that appetite for building hasn't changed." That growth is now happening across locations, too. Stockholm remains home to most of the engineering team, while the New York and London teams are beginning to expand. Oskar and other engineers now spend regular stints in the other offices to help build the team and establish the same culture on the ground. For Oskar, maintaining that culture comes down to being intentional about who joins the team. Legora keeps its hiring bar high, looking for people who share the same standards and excitement for building. “We keep the bar high when we hire. But in return we get this engineering culture with very high standards, which I think is really important if we’re going to succeed.” That same mindset extends to how the team works. Engineers are encouraged to go beyond their immediate remit and take ownership of problems that interest them. Oskar has had much experience doing exactly that, including when he picked up a platform stability issue that wasn’t technically his to solve, simply because he wanted to see if he could fix it. Skills let legal teams encode their standards, processes and preferences inside the Legora aOS™. Today we're launching Skills , available to all Legora customers. Skills enable lawyers to encode their ways of working so the Agent knows how to execute work to their standards. Every legal team knows the law. What sets them apart is how they practice it: the positions they take, how they structure their advice, the tone they strike with the other side. That way of working takes years to build, and it's what makes their work recognizably their own. Some of it sits in playbooks, or in precedents, or in the experienced heads of the lawyers who built them. Skills turns it into instructions the Agent can follow on every task. "What I find valuable about Skills is that it gives us a consistent process while still being flexible. It adapts to the information provided, asks questions when it needs more context, and helps us get to the result we actually need." – Kiren Bigwood, Senior Growth Manager, Hamilton Locke What are Skills? A Skill is a set of natural language instructions, saved as a Markdown file, that teaches the Agent how to approach a specific legal task. It captures three things: the standards your team holds its work to, the processes it follows, and the preferences that make the work recognizably yours. A Skill might set out how you review a supplier agreement against your playbook, including the fallback positions you'll accept on liability and indemnities. It might capture your process for building a trial bundle, or the way a partner likes a client advice note structured. Along with instructions, a Skill can hold reference materials, templates and past examples, including what the output should not look like. The Agent can invoke a Skill when a task calls for it, or you can tell it which Skill to use. You can read, edit, export and update any Skill as your work changes. " I think of a Skill as a packaged capability because it's a package, there's a lot you can put in it: structured instructions, reference materials, your templates, even other Skills ." – Timothy Besada, Software Engineer for the Agent. How Skills work Using a Skill starts the way any work in Legora starts: by prompting the Agent in the chat, in natural language. If a Skill already exists for the task, the Agent recognizes it and uses it automatically. You don't need to find it or name it. To pick a Skill yourself, type / in the chat and choose from the list. If no Skill exists yet, the Agent can build one from documents you've already produced, or by asking you a few questions about how you approach the task. When it's done, it asks whether you want to install the new Skill. Some lawyers spend time refining a Skill until it's exactly right. Others build one in five minutes, with the Agent doing most of the work. Take a litigation team working on a matter with a large case file. The Agent can move and rename files, so the team creates a Skill that sets out how every matter should be organized: the folder structure, the naming conventions, where pleadings and correspondence go. From then on, every new matter is set up the same way. More capable than a prompt. More flexible than a workflow. Prompts, workflows, and Skills all direct the Agent’s work, and each suits a different kind of work. A prompt is an instruction for the task in front of you. It's the quickest way to get work started, and you write it fresh each time. A workflow is a fixed sequence. You run it when a process needs to be followed the same way every time. A Skill is know-how the Agent keeps. You set it up once, and the Agent applies it whenever the work calls for it, adapting to the task at hand. Unlike a prompt, a Skill can carry files su

blogs.content: There is no best model. Bet on the system. | Legora Product Solutions Security Customers Company Log in Book a demo Menu Log in Product Updates There is no best model. Bet on the system. There is no best model. Bet on the system. Category Product Updates published Oct 1, 2026 author Team Legora There is no best model. The frontier is jagged. Advancements are constant, surprising, and uneven. Model advancements are uneven, surprising, and accelerating - just last week, Gemini 3.8 Flash, Muse Spark 1.3, Fable 5.1, and GPT-6 Astra were all released. Every model has unique characteristics (or personalities, if you will) and they excel at different things. As such, no single model will be the best model for everything. But a system that takes advantage of each model’s unique strengths and mitigates its weaknesses can outperform any one model. The frontier is jagged The headline leaderboards models are measured against reduce their capabilities to a single dimension and, over time, make the frontier look like a staircase that’s slowly - or rather, very quickly - being climbed. However, vertical AI companies understand that their domains don’t reduce to singular dimension. Rather they understand that models are multifaceted: They have different characteristics, personalities, and they excel at different tasks. Some models need very specific instructions, while others can handle ambiguity. Some are quick to ask for help/clarification, while some are reluctant to ask at all. Some models are great at long-context reasoning, some are good at manipulating documents, and some are good at instruction-following for writing styles. And this dimension is only one of several. Models differ in cost and latency by a factor of fifty or more. Certain providers are very reliable while others often fail either generally or in odd, specific ways. On top of that there are differences in geographic availability and governance. This makes the frontier of intelligence jagged: different models drive the frontier in different aspects. The frontier moves quickly and unevenly Not only is the frontier jagged, it’s constantly changing. New providers are popping up with new models and even new versions of existing models often have vastly different characteristics than previous versions. And it looks like the rate of change is increasing. One year ago there were for all intents and purposes two labs: OpenAI and Anthropic. Now SpaceXAI, Meta Superintelligence, and Google look like serious competitors. Not to mention that Chinese labs like Z.ai and Moonshot have caught up rapidly with frontier closed-weight labs. The palette of potential models has never been more diverse or faster changing. Just last week, Gemini 3.8 Flash, Muse Spark 1.3, Fable 5.1, and GPT-6 Astra were all released. Frontier leaderboards are changing weekly, and the pareto frontier is being pushed outwards along its entire curve: tiny, efficient models are being released for specialized workflows or certain intelligence-saturated tasks, while big models push the ceiling of intelligence and reasoning. And inference efficiency gains and/or open weights competition leads to frequent steep price cuts: recently OpenAI slashed prices by 80% for their Luna model. The best model is all the models Because models are different and the model landscape is changing so quickly, the best way to ensure optimal outputs for our users is to make sure the best possible model does any given job. Often “best” means that it completes the task at a high level of quality at the lowest possible cost and latency. Achieving this generally means decomposing the problem into constituent parts that different models tackle with their own context windows and specialized tools. Each model has strengths and weaknesses. A multi-model system can trace the outer envelope of them all - taking the best capability in each direction to create a whole that outperforms any individual model. blogs.content: The real cost of legal intake | Legora Product Solutions Security Customers Company Log in Book a demo Menu Log in Product Updates The real cost of legal intake The real cost of legal intake Category Product Updates published Sep 15, 2026 author Walter Myer Giving lawyers new tools inside old processes only speeds up their work, but the real gains come from changing the process itself. Over the last few months I've had dozens of conversations with in-house lawyers about how they work. While every organization is different, three key roles have emerged as a common denominator: the requester, the lawyer, and the general counsel. The requester is someone on the commercial side. They're trying to get a deal signed, a supplier approved, a policy question answered. From where they sit, legal is a step in a process, and they want that step to be fast and low-friction. Then there's the lawyer fielding those requests. The lawyer is the person responding to those requests, for which they need the full context before they can do anything useful. They want to protect the organization from risk while also being commercial, acting as a partner to the business rather than being a blocker. Finally there's the general counsel. The GC cares about matching the team's expertise and capacity to the organization's most important legal needs. To do that job well, they need insight about the kind of work that comes in and how it gets completed. When these three roles slot together, the legal department works like a well-oiled machine. In most of my conversations, what I hear instead is a broken process that fails to protect a legal team's scarcest resource, the attention of its best people. Scoping the request A business stakeholder knows what they want to achieve. They may not know what a lawyer needs to help them get there, and we shouldn't expect them to. When a salesperson pings legal to ask for a quick look at a contract renewal, they attach what they have and assume that's enough. But often it’s missing key additional information, like schedule documents to which the contract refers, processes followed before deciding on the extension, and so on. Intake forms can help, because they steer the requester on what they need to provide. But a fixed set of questions often feels ill-adapted to the wide array of requests that can come through. Make the form too short and legal still has to fill the gaps. Make it too detailed and the requester simply sidesteps the intake form, or sometimes even the legal team altogether. According to Onit's 2023 Enterprise Legal Reputation Report , 67% of enterprise employees admit to bypassing legal, even when they know it breaches policy. The standard should be a flexible system that meets requesters where they are, asking only relevant clarifying questions to gather the context needed by the legal team and nothing more. Performing the work Legal work is not all the same. Some of it is routine and repeatable: standard NDAs, security questionnaires, basic compliance queries. This work follows predictable patterns. It draws on the same precedents every time. The legal judgment involved is real, but it doesn't vary much from one instance to the next. Research carried out by EY has found that 27% of in-house legal professionals' time goes to routine and low-value tasks, rising to 32% in larger functions. Work like this should be streamlined, and increasingly, it can benefit from automation. Other work is genuinely complex: an acquisition, a novel regulatory point, a counterparty pushing back on terms that matter. This work requires a lawyer's full attention. But it doesn't need to start from a blank page. As every lawyer knows, it’s far better to review a strong first pass than to start from scratch. That means resetting the default ways of working for lawyers. blogs.content: Ricardo Anaya on starting out as Legora’s first US legal engineer | Legora Product Solutions Security Customers Company Log in Book a demo Menu Log in Legora voices Ricardo Anaya on starting out as Legora’s first US legal engineer Ricardo Anaya on starting out as Legora’s first US legal engineer Category Legora voices published Sep 9, 2026 author Team Legora Having worked as a lawyer, a client, and in legal technology, Ricardo Anaya was unusually well prepared for what he does today: translating legal workflows and judgment into effective ways of using Legora. That discipline has become known as legal engineering, and Ricardo was ideally placed to help establish it for Legora in the US. He studied law at Universidad del Pacífico in Lima, graduating top of his class, and worked at Baker McKenzie and PwC before landing an in-house role in private equity. But it didn't take long for frustration to set in. The work was repetitive and manual, and it rarely delivered the impact he'd gone into law to make. So he moved sides into investing. Within five months of joining Nexus as legal counsel, Ricardo had taught himself the investment business and earned a place on the deal team as the first lawyer in the firm's history to make that jump. He went on to become founding CFO of Olimpo, a sports betting business Nexus built from inside the fund. Then came Stanford where he earned an MBA. This was followed by a role at Responsiv AI, a legal AI company focused on regulatory compliance. "By the time I came to Legora, I'd been the lawyer, been the client, and worked on the product side," he says. "That's basically the job description for a legal engineer, though nobody called it that yet." Employee number seven in North America Ricardo joined Legora as the founding legal engineer for the US and became Lead about six months later. He was employee number seven in Legora's New York office, and roughly the 80th hire at the company globally, joining at a moment when there was no US legal engineering function and no playbook. This meant there was no local precedent to work from. A blank slate might seem intimidating, but Ricardo didn’t see it that way. "The appeal was that there was nothing here yet,” he explains. "Expanding from the ground up, in the largest legal market in the world, was exactly the kind of ambitious problem I wanted to be part of." Legora now has over 250 employees across the US and works with more than 100,000 legal professionals globally, a scale that makes those early days feel a world away. "I have never worked anywhere with this concentration of genuinely brilliant colleagues," he says. "The culture has a mix I hadn't come across before. Real competitiveness, paired with kindness and a default to helping each other. People want to win, and they want the person next to them to win too." The launch he's proudest of was at an AmLaw 50 firm, a project he steered from pilot through to implementation. From a standing start, more than 1,000 lawyers were using the platform within three months, with weekly active users above 70% of the licensed base. The generic workflow problem Ricardo’s biggest learning so far is that no firm works quite like another, however similar they may look from the outside. Two firms running the same deal type will structure it differently and rely on different precedents. Even what counts as a good first draft varies from one firm to the next. A generic workflow can be technically correct, and still go unused. "The fix was to stop building for the practice area and start building for the firm," he says. His team introduced use case discovery sessions as the first pillar of every rollout. "The first step is to understand how a firm actually does the work, where the judgment sits, and what they would never automate." From there, his team works around how the firm actually operates. blogs.content: Creating more value in less time: How the Managing Partner of Harrison LLP became one of Legora's top power users | Legora Product Solutions Security Customers Company Log in Book a demo Menu Log in Shapers Creating more value in less time: How the Managing Partner of Harrison LLP became one of Legora's top power users Creating more value in less time: How the Managing Partner of Harrison LLP became one of Legora's top power users Category Shapers published Sep 3, 2026 author Team Legora Matthew J. Madsen is the Managing Partner of Harrison LLP, a national law firm that focuses exclusively on helping clients define and achieve their private wealth goals. The firm now has more than 100 attorneys across 12 markets, and counts 14 Fellows of the American College of Trust and Estate Counsel among its ranks. Matthew has spent more than 25 years advising high-net-worth individuals and families on complex estate and wealth transfer planning, as well as charitable giving, and he continues to serve as outside General Counsel to the St. Louis Community Foundation alongside his leadership role. Inside his own firm, Matthew carries a specific title: Harrison LLP 's top power user of Legora. What follows is Matthew's account of the bet he made on AI, what being a power user actually requires, and how he's turned his own habits into a firm-wide strategy. Making innovation the centerpiece of firm strategy Innovation is a defining pillar of Harrison LLP’s direction, with AI emerging as one of its clearest expressions. “I remember when an associate told me about ChatGPT and I thought, 'This is going to change everything,'” Matthew says. Championing AI as managing partner meant owning the uncertainty it created. “An associate asked me, after hearing us talk about Legora, 'Is my job okay?'” Matthew recalls. His answer set the tone for how the firm would think about AI going forward: “If you're spending less time on routine work and more time in the meeting with the client, finding out why she's so passionate about how she wants to leave her legacy, that's more value for everybody.” Getting the rest of the firm on board took care. It started small, a beta test group that met periodically to trade tips and figure out what was actually working. “That group has since become our broader Legora users group,” Matthew says, “so the knowledge-sharing culture that developed early carried over into how we operate now.” The other piece is a nomination process: Legora users at the firm periodically identify a peer they think would genuinely benefit from the tool. “The thinking behind it is that seeing a colleague you respect use something effectively tends to move people more than any top-down push,” Matthew explains. What makes a Legora power user “I have great fun with Legora,” Matthew says. He explains how it isn't a tool he opens for a task and closes when it's done; it runs alongside everything he does. He uses it as an active thinking partner — for research, outlining, drafting, and testing arguments — not as a shortcut, but as a way to move faster toward stronger work. “The moments where I've felt the biggest impact have been in document-heavy situations where volume itself is the enemy,” Matthew says. “When you're reviewing twenty years of trust administration records, or trying to understand how a complex business interest interacts with a long-standing estate plan, everything is findable, eventually. The question is how long it takes, and what that costs.” “Getting there takes time no one can afford to waste,” he says. “Legora has surfaced things that I then confirmed were worth pursuing. In this work, that time doesn't disappear. It goes right back into the analysis that shapes the outcome.” “It's also great for client meetings,” he says, where the real advantage isn't preparation but responsiveness. “It just creates a much better experience. blogs.title: How GCs are Rethinking Legal Work With AI
blogs.author: Harvey Team
blogs.description: Three in-house leaders share how they’re expanding their teams’ capacity while keeping lawyers’ judgment central to the work.
blogs.content: Insights How GCs are Rethinking Legal Work With AI Three in-house leaders share how they’re expanding their teams’ capacity while keeping lawyers’ judgment central to the work. by Harvey Team • Oct 16, 2026 In-house legal teams face a steady stream of work that varies in urgency, complexity, and the judgment required. AI can accelerate first drafts and other preparatory work, giving lawyers more room to focus on decisions that require their deep knowledge of the business. That raises an important question for legal leaders: Which work should the team take on vs. hand off to AI, and where can its lawyers add the most value? At Harvey FORUM in Sydney, Silv Roest, Group Chief Legal, Corporate Affairs, and Sustainability Officer at The Warehouse Group; Andrew Chivers, Regional General Counsel, APAC at Brambles Limited; and Georgette Apostolopoulos, General Counsel at The Star shared what they’re learning as AI becomes part of their teams’ day-to-day work. Their examples offer practical lessons for using AI to change how legal teams work, beyond accelerating individual tasks. Change How the Work is Divided At The Warehouse Group, one of the largest retailing groups in New Zealand, Roest is looking at how a four-lawyer team spends its time. First drafts, summaries, and issue tables are necessary work, but they can make it difficult to reach the questions that need the team’s judgment and knowledge of the business. That makes the division of work a useful place to start. Watch Video Apostolopoulos faced a different capacity challenge at The Star, one of Australia’s leading integrated resort companies. After the legal team downsized, it no longer had an in-house litigator to run an anti-discrimination matter. Her team used AI to help prepare the evidence before asking outside firms for quotes. By preparing the evidence in-house, the team could ask firms to price the work that remained, giving it a way to manage outside counsel costs. Watch Video Both examples start by breaking work into its component steps. Legal leaders can then identify what AI can help prepare, where their lawyers need to apply judgment, and when outside counsel’s expertise is needed. That gives a lean team a clearer way to allocate its time and scope external work. Make Existing Knowledge Easier to Use For a legal team supporting a global business, even a familiar question can take time to answer when the relevant guidance sits across different policies and jurisdictions. Global supply chain logistics company Brambles has 24 lawyers working across 60 countries. Chivers described how his team brought its policies together in an agent that people can query, reducing the need to search through documents each time a question comes in. Watch Video The example offers a useful starting point for teams with knowledge spread across many documents: look for questions that come up repeatedly and require lawyers to consult the same sources. Making those sources easier to use can help the team respond more quickly, while lawyers still assess how the guidance applies to the particular situation. Help Lawyers Evaluate AI Output Making information easier to access also changes the skills lawyers need to practice. Chivers noted that junior lawyers may be comfortable using AI while still developing the legal knowledge needed to challenge its answers. Familiarity with the tool is useful; the ability to spot a missing fact, weak inference, or incorrect conclusion takes training. Watch Video That training can happen in the course of real work. When reviewing an AI-assisted draft, a supervising lawyer can ask a junior colleague what they checked, where the answer came from, and why they agree with it. The discussion helps the junior lawyer develop judgment alongside their ability to use the tool. blogs.content: Meet Anthony Ross, Spellbook’s First Legal Fellow - Spellbook spellbook.legal cookie bridge --> Webinar: The first-ever live demo of Spellbook ACM • Oct. 29 • Save your spot Product Solutions Resources Customers Careers Security Start your 7-day free trial Book a Demo Login Book a Demo Back to Blog Blog / Updates Last Updated on Sep 09, 2026 by Daniel DiMaria Meet Anthony Ross, Spellbook’s First Legal Fellow Earlier this year, we launched our $1 million Spellbook Legal Fellowship Fund to support law students working at the intersection of law and technology. After reviewing 151 applications from students at 61 schools, we are thrilled to announce Anthony Ross, a law student at the University of Missouri–Kansas City School of Law, as our first fellow. Anthony will spend the coming semester, tackling one of M&A’s most notorious workflows: disclosure schedules. With global transaction volumes surging 30% to $2.6 trillion in the first half of 2026, M&A is set for a record-breaking year. That increase in deal volume means a corresponding increase in contract volume. For most deals, preparing disclosure schedules means combing through every relevant contract a company has signed, one by one, to find what needs to be disclosed. It is grueling, high-stakes, needle-in-a-haystack work. But as Anthony put it, the actual lawyering involved is merely a "thin slice of judgment on top of a thick layer of hunting." Drawing on his experience as a summer associate at Polsinelli, Anthony plans to build an AI solution that cleanly separates those layers. His proposed tool will read the data room, surface candidate disclosures, and connect each result to its source language, leaving only the final judgment calls to the lawyer reviewing the results. Anthony will work alongside the Spellbook team to develop and test his idea. Congratulations, Anthony. We’re proud to have you as our first Spellbook Legal Fellow. blogs.description: Legal Work Orchestration brings the phases, tasks, and reviews of a matter or project into the same place as the documents and the agents.
blogs.content: Product Making Harvey the Orchestration Layer for Legal Work Legal Work Orchestration brings the phases, tasks, and reviews of a matter or project into the same place as the documents and the agents. by Harvey Team • Oct 15, 2026 Today, we’re launching Legal Work Orchestration , a new way to organize and manage legal matters in Harvey. It connects the phases, tasks, people, and review points within a matter so that agents can execute defined tasks, lawyers can review their work at designated gates, and everyone involved can see what needs to happen next. Watch Video Much of legal work follows a repeatable process. An M&A transaction, for example, moves through familiar phases, tasks, and review points. But the process itself often has to be reconstructed for every new matter from a checklist, a previous deal, or the knowledge of the people who have done it before. AI agents can already complete many individual steps within that process. What they often lack is the structure around the task: where it fits in the matter, which documents and instructions apply, who should review the output, and what happens next. Lawyers still have to provide that context, move the work between people and systems, and track its progress. Legal Work Orchestration brings that structure into Harvey, allowing lawyers and agents to work through a matter together in one place. How Legal Orchestration Works The same structure can support any matter or project a team runs more than once, from an M&A transaction to a quarterly compliance review. Legal Work Orchestration captures that process in a reusable template, carries the relevant context into each task, and coordinates reviews and next steps. Capture the Process in a Reusable Template Templates capture how your organization runs a recurring type of work. When an associate opens a new buy-side acquisition, the Space can already contain the relevant phases, tasks, playbooks, agents, collaborators, and review gates. Innovation and knowledge teams can define that structure once, helping teams follow a consistent process across matters without rebuilding it from scratch. Give Every Task the Context it Needs Each task includes its scope, inputs, and reviewer. An agent assigned a change-of-control review can therefore analyze the relevant contracts and produce a consent matrix without the lawyer having to assemble a new prompt and briefing for that step. Tasks can also be assigned to another lawyer or shared with the client while retaining the relevant matter context. The work no longer depends on one person manually carrying information from one step to the next. Keep Reviews and Next Steps Moving When the agent completes the review, Harvey notifies the designated partner that the consent matrix is ready. Once the partner approves it, the task is completed and the next step can begin. Updates can also be made from email. A lawyer can ask Harvey in a reply to close a task or begin the next one, while the Space maintains a current view of the matter’s progress. Partners can see where the work stands without asking an associate to reconstruct the status from email and separate checklists. The Future of Legal Work Orchestration Before the release of Harvey II in August, every step delegated to Harvey required a lawyer to gather the documents, write the instructions, and move the output to wherever it needed to go next. Legal Work Orchestration reduces that overhead by giving each task its inputs, instructions, and reviewer in advance. Today, lawyers still actively prompt the majority of steps in a legal workflow. We expect that balance to change rapidly. Over the next six months, we expect agents to take on an additional 20% of workflow steps. Within a year, we expect that share to triple. Lawyers will remain in control through defined review gates, and the work performed by agents will remain transparent and auditable. blogs.content: Legora AI Day at Bucerius Law School: preparing the next generation of lawyers | Legora Product Solutions Security Customers Company Log in Book a demo Menu Log in Legora AI Day at Bucerius Law School: preparing the next generation of lawyers Legora AI Day at Bucerius Law School: preparing the next generation of lawyers Category published Aug 19, 2026 author Team Legora What does it mean to train a lawyer in the age of AI? That question sat at the heart of Legora AI Day at Bucerius Law School, the official launch of Bucerius's campus-wide Legora license and a signal of how seriously one of Europe's leading law schools is taking the transformation of the legal profession. The event brought together students, practicing lawyers, and legal innovators for a day of onboarding sessions and panel discussions about how AI is shaping the legal industry, and what that means for the people entering it. A profession in motion The legal market is changing faster than legal education has traditionally moved. Nathalia Schomerus, Legal Innovation Lead at Legora, explained: "I think students are not being prepared well enough for the age of AI. The way legal work is shifting means that the way we educate future lawyers has to shift as well." Florian Skupin, Executive Director of Legal Technology at Bucerius, agreed: "Legal education will need to adapt more to market realities. It's quite important that our students have AI experience during their studies." From the courtroom to the classroom The day featured practitioners who use Legora in their daily work, giving students a direct line to what AI-assisted legal practice actually looks like. Stefan Papastefanou, Associate at White & Case, made the point that law firms and their clients are already recalibrating expectations around efficiency: "Clients are starting to require you to showcase how much time you've saved." His message to students was to engage with these tools now, build a genuine understanding of what they can do, and come into the profession ready. Jonathan Cholewa, Partnerships and Digital Development at Otto Schmidt, brought a publisher's perspective. As a leading legal content provider, Otto Schmidt's goal is simple: to be present wherever legal research is happening next, and increasingly, that means AI platforms like Legora. It's a reminder that the shift extends beyond law firms and law schools. The entire legal information ecosystem is orienting around where AI-driven research happens. The next generation of lawyers If the practitioners were enthusiastic, the students matched them. "I'm using it on an everyday basis," one student said, when asked about Legora. "I have all of the material from the professors in there. I keep asking it questions and it's helping me so much." Another student added, "AI is becoming really important in the future, and I want to be on top of it." "I see a lot of opportunities," said another. "I want to work with it." That mindset is exactly what firms are looking for. Vadym Kuzmenko, Legal Engineer at Legora, pointed to the practical advantage students gain from starting early: "Coming in already with knowledge of how to use these tools is great for the law firms and the companies because you are quicker to be onboarded. You are quicker to actually deliver value." More than a license What distinguishes this partnership is the intent behind it. As Nathalia put it: "We're not just giving them licenses and then letting them run. I want to make sure that the lawyers we have in the future are the best lawyers." That means preparing students who don't just know how to use a tool, but understand when and why to use it, and how to critically evaluate what it produces. Legora AI Day at Bucerius was a starting point. The campus license means students will be working with Legora throughout their studies, building the kind of fluency that only comes from sustained, real-world use. blogs.description: Teach the Agent how you work. Skills let legal teams encode their standards, processes and preferences inside the Legora aOS™.
blogs.content: KI im Rechtsbereich: Was Teams heute brauchen | Legora Product Solutions Security Customers Company Log in Book a demo Menu Log in Perspectives KI im Rechtsbereich: Was Teams heute brauchen KI im Rechtsbereich: Was Teams heute brauchen Category Perspectives published Oct 13, 2026 author Janusch Krasberg Anfang 2026 arbeiteten rund 3.000 Juristinnen und Juristen in Deutschland mit Legora. Bei der Eröffnung des Münchner Büros Ende September waren es bereits mehr als 13.000. Besonders stark wächst die Nutzung in Rechtsabteilungen: Dort hat sich die Zahl der Nutzenden seit Januar verachtfacht. Deutschland hat den Ruf, neue Technologien eher zögerlich aufzugreifen. Bei KI zeichnet sich ein anderes Bild ab: Kanzleien und Rechtsabteilungen setzen die Technologie mit bemerkenswertem Tempo ein. Für den deutschen Markt reicht es nicht, KI ins Deutsche zu übersetzen. Sie muss auf das deutsche Recht und die Arbeitsweise juristischer Teams ausgerichtet sein. In unseren Gesprächen mit Kanzleien und Rechtsabteilungen in Deutschland, Österreich und der Schweiz verändern sich die Fragen. In ersten Tests von KI-Lösungen für den Rechtsbereich ging es vor allem darum, wie verlässlich KI bei Recherche, Analyse und Entwürfen unterstützt. Inzwischen beschäftigen sich die Teams zunehmend mit der Auswahl eines passenden Anbieters, der Einführung im Team und der Einbindung in bestehende Arbeitsabläufe. Bei der Auswahl einer passenden Lösung zeigt sich in intensiven Pilotphasen, wie gut sie zum eigenen Arbeitsalltag passt. Teams bringen dafür ihre vorhandenen Unterlagen, ihr Wissen und ihre internen Vorgaben ein. Entscheidend ist, wie gut Legora diese Informationen nutzbar macht und sich an die Arbeitsweise des jeweiligen Teams anpasst: wie Ergebnisse aufbereitet werden, wie sie in die weitere Beratung einfließen und wie Kolleginnen und Kollegen damit zusammenarbeiten. Was deutsche juristische Arbeit von KI verlangt Wer Rechts-KI in Deutschland einführt, trifft auf konkrete fachliche Anforderungen. Das beginnt bei der Sprache. Eine juristische Stellungnahme auf Deutsch muss Fachbegriffe präzise verwenden, die relevante Fragestellung erfassen und eine nachvollziehbare Argumentation enthalten. Bei grenzüberschreitenden Mandaten kommen unterschiedliche Arbeitssprachen hinzu. Ein englischsprachiger Vertrag kann die Grundlage für eine deutsche Stellungnahme bilden, die anschließend mit einem internationalen Team abgestimmt wird. Eigene Vertragsmuster und frühere Stellungnahmen ermöglichen es Teams, Entwürfe in Legora an den fachlichen und sprachlichen Standards ihrer Organisation auszurichten. Ebenso entscheidend sind die Rechtsquellen. Gesetze, Rechtsprechung und Kommentarliteratur bilden zusammen mit dem Wissen der jeweiligen Organisation die Grundlage juristischer Arbeit. Für KI-Anwendungen bedeutet das: Der Zugang zu relevanten Inhalten, erkennbare Fundstellen und die Möglichkeit zur Überprüfung müssen im Arbeitsablauf mitgedacht werden. Deutsche Fachverlage spielen deshalb auch bei der Entwicklung von Rechts-KI eine wichtige Rolle. Wer Module von Otto Schmidt abonniert hat, kann diese direkt in Legora nutzen. Hinzu kommt der Umgang mit Daten. Kanzleien und Unternehmen benötigen konkrete Antworten darauf, wo Informationen verarbeitet werden, wer darauf zugreifen kann und wie ihre Verwendung geregelt ist. Datensouveränität und Vertraulichkeit gehören damit an den Anfang der Einführung. Wer Rechts-KI für Deutschland auswählt, sollte ihre Qualität an deutscher juristischer Arbeit messen. Gute Ergebnisse im britischen oder US-amerikanischen Rechtskontext lassen sich nicht ohne Weiteres übertragen. Kanzleien und Rechtsabteilungen sollten deshalb anhand eigener Fälle prüfen, ob eine Lösung relevante deutsche Quellen einbezieht, juristische Begriffe präzise verwendet und ihre Ergebnisse nachvollziehbar belegt. Ebenso muss sie die Anforderungen der Organisation an Vertraulichkeit und Zusammenarbeit erfüllen. Wie Rechtsabteilungen ihren KI-Einsatz weiterentwickel

blogs.content: Insights Building a Frontier In-House Organization How legal teams are transforming their departments with Harvey to better serve the enterprise and help the business move faster. by Matt Zerweck and Gabe Pereyra • Oct 13, 2026 Satya Nadella describes the frontier firm as a company built around intelligence on demand, where people and agents work side by side. Inside most companies, the legal department is where that shift arrives first. For the general counsels we work with, the question used to be how to get lawyers to use AI. Now it’s how to run the department on it. Behind that shift are four challenges we hear from in-house teams: Legal as the bottleneck. Lawyers spend too much time on work that doesn’t need legal judgment, instead of working at the top of their license. Rising volume, flat headcount. Demand for Legal grows with the business but headcount and budgets do not. Reactive instead of proactive. Regulatory change and contract risk surface late, when they’re already problems. No portfolio visibility. Contract history, obligations, and outside matters are scattered across systems, inboxes, and law firms. None of these problems stay in one lane. A single contract can be a bottleneck, a capacity problem, and a visibility gap at once. And when requests queue up and the business can’t see where they stand, employees bypass Legal and take legal questions to general-purpose AI tools, outside Legal’s controls. Banning that doesn't work. The frontier move is to give the business a better place to ask, with Legal in control of the answers. The Platform for a Frontier Legal Department Figure 1. The legal department of a frontier firm with everything in one place. We’re building Harvey as one platform for the business, its legal team, and outside counsel. It connects every request, contract, and matter with the documents, conversations, and context behind it. That knowledge, including the department’s policies, prior decisions, and outcomes, is codified in one legal brain that people and agents draw on as they work. Legal decides what agents can handle and where people should make the call. Legal puts that knowledge to work across requests, contracts, and matters. It sets what agents can handle, where people make the call, and when to involve outside counsel. Past matters, outcomes, and invoice data help Legal choose the right firm for the work. Requests come in and follow-up questions, updates, and completed work go back through the channels the business already uses. Each outcome adds to the department’s knowledge, informing the next decision. Figure 2. The platform architecture. Connected systems feed a shared model of the department’s work, with source permissions preserved. Harvey’s products and agents draw on that same model. If a sales lead asks whether a customer deal can include a new AI-use clause, Harvey can pull up the original request, the department’s position on AI clauses, the terms the company has agreed to before, and the EU rules that apply, all in one answer. We've built that connectivity with partners over several years. Harvey runs on Microsoft Azure and works inside Microsoft 365 , from Word to Copilot Cowork. It connects to LexisNexis for primary law, to Docusign and Ironclad for contract workflows, and through the Connector Library to the rest of the systems the department already uses. Resolve Requests Wherever the Business Works Intake extends the department’s legal front door across email, chat, and business systems, including Outlook, Gmail, Slack, Teams, Jira, ServiceNow, and Salesforce. Harvey gathers context, then routes and assigns work by type, risk, and department. Agents and lawyers send follow-up questions, updates, and completed work back through the same channels. Figure 3. Three paths for a request, with Legal setting the rules. Answers and completed work return to the business. Adapted from Winston Weinberg’s FORUM New York in-house keynote. blogs.content: Company Harvey to Open Tokyo Office by Harvey Team • Oct 12, 2026 Harvey will open an office in Tokyo in early 2027, deepening our commitment to supporting law firms and in-house legal teams in Japan. Trust is earned over time through close collaboration and consistent support. As we grow in Japan, we are investing in a local presence to build lasting relationships, listen to our customers, and ensure their needs guide how we continue to build and grow here. Our Tokyo office will support our growing customer base in Japan and deepen relationships with law firms including Mori Hamada & Matsumoto and Nagashima Ohno & Tsunematsu, and in-house legal teams, including Mitsubishi Corporation. A local presence will help us work more closely with these teams and strengthen the support we provide. We are also building Harvey to better support work in Japanese and reflect the needs of legal professionals in Japan. This includes our partnership with Legalscape for Japanese legal research. Working with local experts and listening to customer feedback will help guide how we develop our product and support its use. “Japan is a critical market for legal and home to many exceptional law firms and companies. With the government investing in AI acceleration country-wide, there’s no better time to bring Harvey to Tokyo,” said Winston Weinberg, Harvey’s Chief Executive Officer. “Having a team in Japan will help us better understand the needs of legal professionals in Japan and make their experience central to how we build and grow here.” Koji Toshima, Partner and CFO, Mori Hamada & Matsumoto, said, “Since establishing our partnership with Harvey in 2024, we have worked closely together to explore how AI can enhance the quality and efficiency of legal services in Japan. Harvey’s decision to open a Tokyo office is a very welcome and significant milestone, demonstrating its strong commitment to the Japanese legal market. Building on our collaboration to date, including our recent support in bringing about the partnership between Harvey and Legalscape, we look forward to further strengthening our collaboration with Harvey to advance the development of innovative AI solutions tailored to the needs of Japanese legal practice and deliver even greater value to our clients in Japan and around the world.” Tokyo will expand Harvey’s existing presence across Asia-Pacific, alongside our teams in Sydney, Singapore, and Bengaluru. Globally, more than 3,500 customers in over 85 countries use Harvey. We are grateful for the trust our customers in Japan have placed in us and look forward to building on our work here, alongside the lawyers and legal teams we serve. blogs.content: How Grant Thornton UK is delivering sharp client insights in high-stakes forensic work | Legora Product Solutions Security Customers Company Log in Book a demo Menu Log in Case Study How Grant Thornton UK is delivering sharp client insights in high-stakes forensic work How Grant Thornton UK is delivering sharp client insights in high-stakes forensic work Category Case Study published Aug 12, 2026 author Team Legora Grant Thornton UK’s Forensic and Investigation Services team regularly works across borders, under pressure, and with data sets that continue to grow dramatically in scale and complexity. Clients expect clear, defensible insights and they need them fast. By embedding Legora across its forensic workflows, Grant Thornton has augmented how its team navigates large volumes of data, enabling investigators to spend more time on the judgment-intensive analysis that defines exceptional client work. With Legora, Grant Thornton: Enhanced document review with AI-assisted analysis across email, contract, and multi-language data sets Embedded Legora into the team’s established, practitioner-led review process, helping to surface inconsistencies and contradictions for review – supporting, not replacing, professional judgment Enabled the team to get to judgment-led inquiry earlier in each project, supporting the quality and robustness of insights delivered to clients The challenge: scale, speed, and the demand for rigor Forensic and investigation work has always been data-intensive. But for Kathryn Karssiens, Director in Grant Thornton UK’s Forensic and Investigation Services team, the challenge has shifted considerably over the course of her career. “The volume of data that I'm seeing now versus back then is massive. It's such a big change,” she explains. “Data sets have become more international and timelines have become tighter.” In practice, this created a compounding set of pressures. Large volumes of documents – such as emails, contracts and other records – needed to be reviewed quickly and accurately, often across languages, and always to the standard that high-stakes forensic work demands. Before Legora, the team already used sophisticated e-discovery and review technologies to manage large datasets. The challenge was not accessing the information but understanding it quickly. The team often spent significant time familiarizing themselves with unfamiliar data; foreign-language documents drew on colleagues with the right language skills or trusted external translators, and contract comparisons involved detailed side-by-side analysis. “It was a thorough process,” Kathryn says, “but it was time-intensive and fairly dependent on specialist resources being available.” The result was that a significant portion of every project was spent simply getting oriented before the team could move on to the higher-value work of interpreting findings, applying professional judgment and helping clients make informed decisions. From pilot to practice Kathryn arranged a demonstration of Legora with a few colleagues. “Everyone that used it could immediately see how it would take the heavy lifting out of the process,” she recalls. Following a pilot phase that ran across several teams within the forensic practice, Legora was adopted more broadly. Translation became one of the most significant use cases early on. Rather than coordinating internal resources or engaging third parties, the team now runs multi-language document sets through Legora directly, handling a range of languages and feeding reliable outputs straight into the review process. On one project, the team needed to translate a set of foreign language documents as part of a broader review. Previously, this would have involved drawing on colleagues with the right language expertise, getting them set up on the project, and absorbing the delay. With Legora, the team was able to generate an initial translation quickly, before carrying out a quality check to validate accuracy and context.

blogs.title: 60% of SEC-Filed Contracts Contain Errors | Spellbook Labs
blogs.description: Spellbook Labs analyzed 3,000+ public-company agreements across 520 organizations. Sixty percent had drafting errors.
blogs.content: 60% of SEC-Filed Contracts Contain Errors | Spellbook Labs spellbook.legal cookie bridge --> Overview Findings at a Glance Issues by Company Issues by Founding Decade Issues by Industry Issues by Contract Type Issues by Filing Year Conclusion Methodology and Scope Humans Hallucinate Too Humans Hallucinate Too. 60% of SEC-Filed Contracts Contain Errors Spellbook Labs analyzed 60,000 pages of public-company agreements across 520 organizations. Sixty percent of contracts had drafting errors. When a self-driving car crashes, it makes the news. The scrutiny is warranted, but the headlines obscure the baseline. Human drivers cause far more crashes . They happen every day, yet almost none become media stories. In legal work, AI hallucinations also get the headlines. An AI-generated legal brief citing non-existent case studies. A judge who used AI to create a restraining order and misquoted state law. These are real issues that deserve attention. But Spellbook sees a different side to AI’s impact on legal and contract workflow. We see the human mistakes that are made when volume and complexity are met with limited hours and manual review. In fact, our data shows saved hours, greater accuracy and increased output when AI is deployed. So we decided to dig into the data to prove what we already know intuitively—humans make mistakes too. Using Spellbook Reviews, we analyzed 3,000+ SEC-filed contracts from over 500 companies, spanning 22 years. These were executed agreements from some of the largest and most heavily lawyered companies in the world. The findings showed plenty of interesting trends and fun examples. Six in ten contracts contained drafting issues. Many were minor. But one in 40 was high-risk—defined as changing the meaning of an agreement in a substantially negative way for at least one party—and they were concentrated in provisions that decide who gets paid, who carries the liability, and what happens in a dispute. None of this is a matter of carelessness by lawyers so much as a consequence of the length, complexity, and disjointed nature of how these types of SEC-filed agreements are prepared and negotiated. In this context, mistakes are inevitable. But they don’t have to be. Every company, public or private, will eventually run its contracts through products like Spellbook that will not only spot errors and risks immediately but suggest fixes based on a company’s own agreement context and real-time market data. Issue Example: A loan cap written two different ways. A mining company's loan agreement set its borrowing limit at "One Million Five-Hundred Sixty Thousand Dollars," then printed the figure beside it as $1,750,000.00. The words and the number differ by $190,000, and the mismatch appears twice. If the borrower and lender ever disagree, the contract gives a court no clear answer, and $190,000 turns on who wins. Findings at a Glance This study should be treated as a proxy for how much humans miss. We kept our analysis deliberately narrow, counting only objective drafting mistakes we could verify from the document itself. We could not judge whether an agreement was signed out of policy, drifted off market, or if a company gave away more than it should, let alone what sits inside the millions of private contracts. These numbers should be thought of as the floor, not a full account of everything worth fixing in an agreement. A full explanation of the review process, including how we defined and classified issues, appears in Methodology and Scope . 01 Some of the world's most valuable companies had the messiest contracts Skip to Section 02 No industry was issue-free, but Media, Telecom, and Travel fared the worst Skip to Section 03 Old established companies made fewer drafting errors Skip to Section 04 The riskiest issues clustered in purchase agreements Skip to Section 05 Human review hasn’t improved in the last 20+ years Skip to Section Issue Example: An emotional outburst left in a corporate charter.
